title: Air around us: we cannot see it, but we can feel it

summary.text: Sit very still with the fan off, and you feel no air at all. Yet a plastic bag swept under the bed comes back puffed up and full. Air is all around us, in every corner, even where a place looks empty. We cannot see it, because light goes straight through it. We feel it when it moves against our skin, and we see what moving air pushes. Humans and other animals breathe it, and plants take it in through their leaves.
summary.art: A child pulling a puffed-up plastic bag out from under a bed, with a second child sitting very still on the bed with eyes closed, and a curtain moving at the window.

intro.hook: Hold your hand in front of your face and look between your fingers. Can you see anything there? Now wave your other hand fast near your cheek. What did you feel?
intro.text: You saw nothing, but you felt something. That something is air. Air is all around us, but we cannot see it. In this unit we catch air in a bag in every corner of the home. We find out when our skin can feel air, and when it cannot. And we watch what moving air can push.
intro.art: A child looking at her open hand with a puzzled face, while her other hand waves near her cheek and her hair lifts a little.

outcomes: By the end I can say that air is all around us, in every corner of our home, even where it looks empty.
By the end I can say that we cannot see air, but we can feel it when it moves.
By the end I can say that wind is moving air, and point to things that moving air pushes.
By the end I can catch air in a bag and feel it push back.
By the end I can say that humans and other animals breathe air, and that plants take it in too.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Air is all around us. It fills every space that looks empty. We cannot see it, but we can feel it when it moves.
terms.example: There is air in your room, under your bed and inside an empty bucket.
terms.art: A cosy room drawn with a very faint sparkle filling every corner: under the bed, inside a cupboard, inside a bucket.

terms.meaning: Invisible means we cannot see it. Air is invisible because light goes straight through it.
terms.example: Clean air in your room is invisible. You look right through it and see the wall.
terms.art: A clear glass of water and a window, with a child looking through both at a tree outside.

terms.meaning: Wind is air that is moving. We cannot see the wind, but we can see what it pushes.
terms.example: The wind sways the coconut trees and flaps the clothes on the balcony line.
terms.art: Coconut palms bending one way and clothes flapping on a balcony line.

terms.meaning: To breathe is to take air into your body and let it out again. You do it all day and all night.
terms.example: When you breathe in, your chest gets bigger. When you breathe out, warm air comes out of your nose.
terms.art: A child with a hand on their chest, breathing in, with a soft curl of air going into the nose.

explanations.context: This card says what air is and where it is, after catching air in a bag.
explanations.definition: Air is a real thing that fills the space around us, indoors and outdoors, all over the Earth.
explanations.description: A room that looks empty is full of air. So is the space under your bed, inside a cupboard and inside an empty bottle. Air is made of tiny bits, far too small to see, and it wraps the whole Earth like a blanket.
examples: A plastic bag swept under the bed comes out puffed up with air.
An empty bottle with no cap is full of air.
Mountain climbers on very high mountains carry extra oxygen in cylinders to breathe, because the air up there is thin.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a flat, with tiny dots of air filling every room, under the bed and inside the cupboards, and the Earth wrapped in a thin blue layer in a small circle in the corner.

explanations.context: This card explains why air is invisible.
explanations.definition: Something is invisible when light goes straight through it, so nothing comes back to our eyes.
explanations.description: We see a thing when light bounces off it into our eyes. Light goes straight through a little clean air, so we see what is behind it. But a huge amount of air sends back some blue light. That is why the sky looks blue, and when you look up, you are seeing air.
examples: You can see the tree through a clean window, but you hardly see the glass.
Hills far away look a little blue, because there is a lot of air between you and them.
The sky is blue in the day. Where there is no air, out in space, the sky is black.
explanations.art: A child looking up at a bright blue sky, with a faint drawing of tiny air bits high up sending blue light down to her eyes.

explanations.concept: We feel air when it moves
explanations.context: This card explains why we feel air only sometimes, after the still-and-moving test.
explanations.definition: We feel air when it moves against our skin, or when we move through it. Moving air is called wind.
explanations.description: The tiny bits of air touch your skin all the time, from every side. When the air is still, you do not notice it. When air moves, it bends the tiny hairs on your arms and presses your skin, and you feel it.
examples: Sitting still with the fan off, you feel no air on your arm.
When you run, you feel air on your face, even on a still day.
A hand fan, like a palm-leaf visari in Kerala, pushes air onto your face.
explanations.art: A child's arm with tiny hairs bending as wavy wind lines pass over it, and a hand fan beside it.

explanations.context: This card is about what wind can do, even though we cannot see it.
explanations.definition: Moving air pushes on whatever is in its way. The faster it moves, the harder it pushes.
explanations.description: We cannot see wind, but we can see what it pushes. A gentle breeze sways a curtain. A strong wind bends trees and flies kites. Air from your mouth can push a cotton ball or a paper boat.
examples: Kites fly high over Ahmedabad at Uttarayan, held up by the wind.
Tall windmills near Kanyakumari turn in the strong wind and make electricity.
A puff of breath pushes a soap bubble across the room.
explanations.art: A row of pictures: a curtain swaying, a kite in the sky, a windmill turning, and a soap bubble drifting.

explanations.context: This card is about who uses air.
explanations.definition: Breathing is taking air into the body and letting it out again. Humans and other animals breathe all day and all night.
explanations.description: You breathe air in through your nose and mouth, and out again. You do it even when you are asleep. A cat, a crow and a cow breathe air too. A fish takes in the air mixed into water through her gills. Plants take in air through tiny holes in their leaves.
examples: Put your hand on your chest and breathe in. Feel your chest get bigger.
A fish in a bowl keeps opening and closing her gills, taking in the air mixed into the water.
A tulsi plant on the balcony takes in air through tiny holes under the leaves.
explanations.art: A child, a cat, a crow, a fish in a bowl and a potted tulsi plant, each with a soft curl of air going in.

agreed.text: Air is a real thing that fills every space that looks empty.
agreed.evidence: A bag swept through any corner of a room fills up with air and pushes back when you squeeze it. A bag squeezed flat and twisted shut stays flat.
We cannot see air, but we see wind push leaves, clothes and kites. A fan or a waving hand makes a small wind that we feel on our skin.

agreed.text: Humans and other animals need air to live, and plants take in air too.
agreed.evidence: We breathe in and out all day and all night, even asleep. Scientists have seen the tiny holes in leaves that let air in and out.

challenging.claim: An empty bottle has nothing inside it.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: We cannot see anything inside it, and it feels light.
challenging.against: The bottle is full of air. Squeeze an open empty bottle near your cheek, and you feel the air rush out.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that an empty-looking bottle holds nothing.

challenging.claim: Trees make the wind by waving their branches.
challenging.who: Many young children. Jean Piaget, a scientist who studied how children think, heard many children say this about 100 years ago.
challenging.for: When we feel a strong wind, we usually see the trees waving too.
challenging.against: Wind blows over the open sea, where there are no trees. A fan makes wind in a room with no trees. On a still day, the trees are still. The wind moves the trees, not the other way round.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many young children make about where wind comes from.

challenging.claim: There is air only outdoors, where the wind blows.
challenging.who: A common guess among young children
challenging.for: Outdoors we often feel the wind. Indoors with the fan off, we feel nothing.
challenging.against: A bag swept through a still room, under a bed or inside a cupboard fills with air. The air indoors is just not moving, so we do not feel it.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess that air lives only outside.

big_questions.q: You cannot see air, but you can feel it. What else is real that you cannot see?
big_questions.hint: Think about smells, sounds and warmth.

big_questions.q: If air is pressing on you all the time, why don't you feel it when you sit still?
big_questions.hint: Think about sitting still, then running.

big_questions.q: The air you breathe out goes into the room, then out of the window. Who might breathe it in next?
big_questions.hint: Think about your family, a crow outside the window and a plant.

big_questions.q: The sky is blue, and the sky is air. So can we see air after all?
big_questions.hint: Think about a little air in a room, and a huge pile of air above us.

story.title: Ammamma's Visari in the Power Cut
story.note: Meenu, Appu and Ammamma are made up. A visari is a hand fan in Malayalam. Palm-leaf hand fans are still sold in many Indian markets.
text: It was a hot afternoon in May, in a flat in Kochi. Meenu was six. Her little brother Appu was four. Their grandmother, Ammamma, was looking after them.
Suddenly the ceiling fan slowed down and stopped. The fridge went quiet. "Power cut," said Ammamma. "It will come back soon."
Without the fan, the room felt hot and sticky. Appu lay flat on the cool floor. Meenu fanned her face with her hand, but she soon got tired.
Ammamma took a palm-leaf fan from the shelf. It was a visari, round and light, with a bamboo handle. She waved it slowly near Meenu's face.
"Aah," said Meenu, closing her eyes. "That's lovely. Ammamma, what is touching my face?"
"What do you think it is?" asked Ammamma.
Meenu opened her eyes and looked at the visari. She looked at the space between the visari and her face. There was nothing there. "I can't see anything," she said. "But something is touching me."
"Hold out your hand," said Ammamma. "Close your eyes. Tell me when you feel it."
Meenu held out her hand. Ammamma waited. Then she waved the visari, once.
"Now!" said Meenu.
Ammamma waited again. She did not wave. Meenu kept quiet. Then Ammamma waved twice. "Now, now!" said Meenu.
"You are right every time," said Ammamma. "What you feel is air. Air is all around us. My visari pushes the air, and the moving air rushes against your skin."
Meenu frowned. "But when you stop, the air goes away."
"Does it?" said Ammamma. "Sit very still. Don't move at all."
Meenu sat as still as a stone. She felt nothing on her hand. Then she waved her other hand near it, and felt a little breeze at once.
"Oh!" said Meenu. "The air didn't go away. It was here all the time. I only feel it when it moves."
"Yes," said Ammamma, smiling. "The air is touching you right now, all over. You notice it only when it moves."
Meenu looked out of the window. The coconut palms were swaying. The clothes on the next balcony were flapping. A crow sat on the wall with her feathers ruffled up.
"The wind is pushing all of them," said Meenu. "So the wind is just air that is moving!"
Appu sat up. "Is there air under the bed too?"
"Go and feel," said Ammamma.
Appu crawled under the bed and waved his hand. "Air!" he shouted. Meenu opened the cupboard and waved her hand inside. "Air in here too!"
Ammamma laughed. "Everywhere you go, the air is there first. It is even inside you. Put your hand on your chest and breathe in."
Meenu breathed in. Her chest grew bigger under her hand. She breathed out slowly onto her palm. It felt warm.
"That air was inside me," she whispered. "Now it's in the room."
Just then, the ceiling fan whirred and began to turn. The power was back.
Meenu lay down next to Appu under the fan. The cool air poured over them. "Ammamma," she said, "the fan is doing your job now."
"Good," said Ammamma, and put the visari back on the shelf. "My arm needs a rest."
story.epiphany: Meenu sits very still and feels no air, then waves her hand and feels it at once. She works out that the air was there all the time, and she feels it only when it moves.
ask: What was touching Meenu's face when Ammamma waved the visari?
Why did Meenu feel nothing when she sat very still?
Where did Appu and Meenu find air in the flat?
art: A grandmother in a cotton saree waving a round palm-leaf fan near a girl's face, while a small boy lies on the cool floor of a flat.
A girl sitting very still with her eyes closed and her hand held out, and the grandmother holding the fan still beside her.
A boy crawling under a bed waving his hand, and the girl waving her hand inside an open cupboard, with coconut palms swaying outside the window.

games.title: See It or Feel It? A sorting card game
games.context: This is a card game about air. You sort cards into three groups: things you can see and feel, things you can feel but not see, and things you can see but not touch. Air goes in the middle group.

items.b: I can see it and feel it.
I can see it and feel it.
I can see it and feel it.
I can see it and feel it.
I can feel it, but I can't see it.
I can feel it, but I can't see it.
I can feel it, but I can't see it.

items.f: The air coming out of a squeezed bag
items.b: I can feel it, but I can't see it.
I can see it, but I can't touch it.
I can see it, but I can't touch it.
I can see it, but I can't touch it. It is too far away.
I can see it, but I can't touch it. It is very, very far away.

printables.title: 3 sorting mats to draw or print
items: I can see it and feel it (draw an eye and a hand)
I can feel it, but I can't see it (draw a hand only)
I can see it, but I can't touch it (draw an eye only)

rules: Lay the three mats on the floor.
Mix the cards and put them face down.
Take turns. Pick up a card, and the grown-up reads it aloud.
Put the card on the mat you think is right, and say why.
Turn the card over to check. If you were right, keep the card. If you were wrong, put the card on the mat where it belongs, and nobody keeps it.
When all the cards are used, count your cards. The most cards wins. A tie is fine: you all win.

setup.art: Three paper mats on a floor, one with an eye and a hand, one with only a hand, one with only an eye.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats.

setup.art: A child putting a card that says 'A breeze on my face' on the mat with only a hand.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card and put it on a mat. Say why.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and draw the three mats. Read the mats aloud.
flow.say: Some things we can see and feel. Some we can only feel. Some we can only see. Let's sort them.
flow.kid: Look at the three mats. One has an eye and a hand. One has a hand. One has an eye.

flow.do: Play the game. Read each card aloud. Ask why before turning it over.
flow.say: Where does this card go? Why do you think so? Let's turn it over and check.
flow.kid: Pick a card. Where does it go? Say why.

ask.q: Where does 'The air from a fan' go? Why?
good: On the hand mat, because I can feel it but not see it.

flow.parent: A child may put 'my shadow' on the see-and-feel mat. Ask them to try to pick up their shadow.

flow.do: Look at the hand-only mat together.
flow.say: Look at the cards on the hand-only mat. What are they all?
flow.kid: Look at the hand-only cards. What are they all?

check.q: All the cards on the hand-only mat are about one thing. What is it?
check.why: The fan, the breeze, your breath and the squeezed bag are all moving air. We feel air when it moves, but we cannot see it.

games.title: Cotton Ball Race: move it with air only
games.context: This is a race on the floor. You move a cotton ball from the start line to the finish line using only moving air. You may not touch it.

printables.title: Race score sheet
items: Round 1: fan it with a notebook. How many waves?
Round 2: blow it. How many blows?
Round 3: puff it with a squeezed bag. How many squeezes?

rules: Put a line of tape or a chappal at the start, and another two big steps away for the finish.
Each player puts a cotton ball on the start line, in their own lane.
Move your cotton ball to the finish line using only air. Don't touch it with anything.
Count your waves, blows or squeezes. The fewest wins the round.
Play three rounds: a notebook fan, your breath, then a bag of air (catch a bagful first, as in Catch the Air). If two players tie in a round, both win it.
Whoever wins the most rounds is the champion. If you play with one other person, a tie is fine.

setup.art: Two cotton balls on a tiled floor next to a line of tape, with another line two big steps away.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cotton balls on the start line.

setup.art: A child kneeling and waving a notebook at a cotton ball rolling along the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Move it with air only. Count your waves.

flow.do: Make the start and finish lines. Give each player a cotton ball and a notebook.
flow.say: We will move these cotton balls with air only. No touching. Count how many waves you need.
flow.kid: Move your cotton ball with air. No touching! Count your waves.
flow.parent: No cotton wool? Use a small, loose ball of scrunched tissue or paper.

flow.do: Play the three rounds. Write each player's count on the score sheet.
flow.say: Round two: blow it! Round three: catch air in a bag and puff it out at your ball.
flow.kid: Fan it. Then blow it. Then puff it with a bag.

flow.do: Ask the last question.
flow.say: Nobody touched the cotton balls. So what pushed them?
flow.kid: Nobody touched the balls. What pushed them?

good: Moving air from the notebook and from my breath.

experiments.title: Catch the Air: is there air in every corner of our home?
experiments.context: In this experiment you try to catch air in a plastic bag in six places in your home. Some of them look empty. You find out if every place has air, and you feel the air you caught.
experiments.question: Is there air everywhere in our home, even in places that look empty, like under the bed or inside an empty bucket?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the bag catch air in every place? Is there any place with no air at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same bag every time. We open it the same way, scoop it in one big sweep, and twist the neck three times. Only the place changes. First we squeeze the bag flat and twist it shut, to see what a bag with no air looks like.
results_table: My guess: is there air here? Yes or no
Did the bag puff up? Yes or no
What did I feel when I squeezed it?

materials.item: a thin plastic carry bag with no holes, about as big as a school bag (or a big zip bag)
paper and crayons, for the results table

experiments.safety: Never put a plastic bag over anyone's head or face. After the experiment, put the bag away where small children cannot reach it.

schedule.what: Guess which places have air. Catch air in a bag in six places. Squeeze each bagful and feel it.

experiments.record: The results table: six places, the guess for each, and a tick if the bag puffed up. Draw the fattest bag.

setup.art: A flat, empty plastic bag held up by a child, next to a paper with six boxes drawn on it.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the flat bag. Guess which places have air.

setup.art: A child sweeping an open plastic bag under a bed, and pulling it out puffed up.
setup.caption: 2. Sweep the open bag through the place. Twist the neck shut.

setup.art: A child squeezing a puffed-up, twisted bag between both hands, with the bag bulging out between her fingers.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze the bag. Feel it push back.

setup.art: A child letting air out of a bag onto her own cheek, with her hair lifting a little.
setup.caption: 4. Let the air out onto your cheek. Feel it.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the flat, empty bag. 2. Name the six places. They are the middle of the room, under the bed and inside a cupboard. Then inside the empty bucket, behind a door, and a corner near the floor. 3. Draw the results table together.
flow.say: We are going to try to catch air in this bag, in six places. Some places look empty, like under the bed. Will the bag catch air everywhere? Is any place empty of air? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will the bag catch air in every place? Is any place empty? Why?

ask.q: Which places will have air? Why?
good: The middle of the room, because it is open.
Not under the bed, because it is dark and closed.
Not inside the bucket, because it is empty.

flow.parent: Write down the guess for each place. Don't say what will happen. Many children guess there is no air under the bed, in a closed cupboard or in an empty bucket.

flow.do: 1. Squeeze the bag flat with your hands. 2. Twist the neck shut three times. 3. Ask your child to pull the sides of the bag and try to make it fat.
flow.say: First, a bag with no air. I squeeze it flat and twist it shut. Now try to make it fat by pulling the sides.
flow.kid: Squeeze the bag flat. Twist it shut. Can you make it fat now?

good: There is nothing inside to make it fat.

flow.parent: The bag stays flat and crinkly. This shows what a bag looks like when nothing has gone in. Keep it in mind for the next step.

flow.do: 1. Untwist the bag and open it wide. 2. In the first place, sweep the open bag through the air in one big scoop. 3. Twist the neck shut three times. 4. Look, then squeeze. 5. Mark the table. 6. Press the air out and go to the next place.
flow.say: Open the bag wide. Sweep it through, in one big scoop. Twist it shut. Did it puff up? Now the next place.
flow.kid: Open the bag. Sweep it through. Twist it shut. Is it fat?
flow.parent: Under the bed: hold the bag open with both hands, push it under, and pull it out fast. In the cupboard and the bucket, scoop the bag right inside. If a bag is only half full, scoop again, a little faster. Every place fills the bag.

flow.do: 1. Catch one more bagful in the middle of the room. 2. Press the full bag gently on the table with both hands. 3. Hold the neck near your child's cheek, untwist it a little and squeeze slowly.
flow.say: Press the bag. Does it push back? Now close your eyes. I'll let the air out near your cheek. Tell me what you feel.
flow.kid: Press the fat bag. Does it push back? Close your eyes. What do you feel on your cheek?

ask.q: What did you feel on your cheek?
good: Air coming out of the bag.

flow.parent: The full bag pushes back like a soft pillow. The air rushing out lifts the hair near the cheek. Keep the bag away from the nose and mouth.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason.
flow.say: What did you find out? Which places had air? How do you know? Were any of your guesses different?
flow.kid: Which places had air? How do you know?

ask.q: Was there any place with no air?
good: No. The bag puffed up every time.
Even under the bed had air.

check.q: The bag puffed up under the bed and inside the empty bucket. What does that show?
options: There is air even in places that look empty
check.why: The flat, twisted bag stayed flat because nothing could get in. The open bag puffed up everywhere because it scooped up air that was already there. Air fills every space that looks empty.

experiments.title: Where Does Your Skin Feel Air Best?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up makes a small puff of air near different parts of your body, while your eyes are shut. You say when you feel it. Then you find out which parts of your skin feel moving air best.
experiments.question: Which part of my skin feels a small puff of air best: my palm, the back of my hand, my cheek, my arm or the sole of my foot?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which part of you will feel the air best? Which part will feel it least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The grown-up uses the same notebook, waves it once each time, and holds it one hand-span from the skin. Each place gets 3 real waves and 1 pretend wave with no air, in a mixed-up order. Your eyes stay shut the whole time.
results_table: Did I say yes to the pretend wave?

materials.item: a notebook or a folded newspaper, to wave

schedule.what: With eyes shut, feel small puffs of air on five parts of the skin. Count how many you felt.

experiments.record: The results table, and a drawing of yourself with a big tick on the part that felt the air best.

setup.art: A child sitting on a mat with eyes closed and one bare arm held out, and a grown-up holding a notebook one hand-span away.
setup.caption: 1. Shut your eyes. Hold out the part to test.

setup.art: A grown-up waving a notebook once beside a child's cheek, with small wind lines between them.
setup.caption: 2. The grown-up waves once. Say 'yes' if you feel it.

flow.do: Show your child the five places to test. They are the palm, the back of the hand, the cheek, the arm and the foot's sole. Draw the table.
flow.say: I will wave this notebook near your skin, without touching. Which part do you think will feel the air best? Which least? Why?
flow.kid: Which part will feel the air best? Which least? Why?

ask.q: Which part will feel it best? Why?
good: My hand, because I touch things with it.
My cheek, because it is soft.

flow.parent: Write the guess down. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes. 2. For each place, wave the notebook once, one hand-span away, three times, with a pretend wave mixed in. 3. For a pretend wave, move your arm but keep the notebook far away. 4. Write each answer.
flow.say: Eyes shut. Say 'yes' when you feel air. Ready? Here comes the next one.
flow.kid: Keep your eyes shut. Say 'yes' when you feel air.
flow.parent: The pretend waves keep the test fair, so we know your child is not just guessing. Waving gently is better than waving hard, so that there is a difference to find.

flow.do: Look at the table together.
flow.say: Which part felt the air most often? Which part felt it least? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Which part felt the air best? Was your guess right?

ask.q: Why do you think that part felt it best?

check.q: The grown-up never touched your skin. What did you feel?
options: Moving air pushed by the notebook
check.why: The notebook pushed the air, and the moving air pressed on your skin. You felt air you could not see.

flow.parent: Many children feel the air best on the cheek and on the arm, where tiny hairs bend in the moving air. The thick skin on the sole of the foot often feels it least. Your child's results may differ, and that is fine.

activities.title: Still Air, Moving Air: when can you feel it?
activities.context: In this activity you sit very still and check if you can feel air on your skin. Then you move the air in different ways and feel it again.

materials.item: a room with the fan off and the windows closed for a few minutes

schedule.what: Sit still and feel for air. Then wave, blow, walk fast and spin, and feel for air each time.

activities.record: Draw yourself sitting still, and yourself running. Show where you felt air.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed and arms resting on her knees, with the ceiling fan stopped.
setup.caption: 1. Sit very still. Can you feel any air?

setup.art: The same child walking fast across the room, with her hair lifting and small wind lines on her face.
setup.caption: 2. Move the air. Wave, blow, walk fast. Feel it now?

flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan and close the windows. 2. Wait a minute. 3. Sit still with your child, eyes closed.
flow.say: Sit very still and close your eyes. Can you feel any air on your arms or your face?
flow.kid: Sit very still. Close your eyes. Can you feel air?
flow.parent: Most children feel nothing. That is what we want them to notice.

flow.do: Try four things, one at a time. Wave a hand near your cheek. Blow on the back of your hand. Walk fast across the room. Spin slowly with your arms out.
flow.say: Now wave your hand near your cheek. Now blow on your hand. Now walk fast. Can you feel air now?
flow.kid: Wave your hand near your cheek. Blow on your hand. Walk fast. Feel it?

ask.q: When could you feel the air?

flow.do: Ask the last question.
flow.say: When you sat still, was there air in the room?
flow.kid: When you sat still, was the air still there?

check.q: You sat still and felt no air. Then you waved and felt air at once. What does that show?
options: The air came in when you waved
The air was there all the time, and you felt it when it moved
There is no air in a still room
check.why: Waving does not make air. It moves the air that was already there. You feel air when it moves against your skin.

activities.title: Blow Painting: see what air does
activities.context: In this activity you put a drop of runny paint on paper and blow it with a straw. You can't see your breath, but you can see what it does to the paint.

materials.item: runny paint: watercolour or poster paint mixed with water, or a spoon of haldi in a little water
a straw, or a sheet of paper rolled into a thin tube

activities.safety: Blow out through the straw. Never suck in.

schedule.what: Put drops of runny paint on paper. Blow them with a straw to make a picture.

activities.record: Your blow painting. Write or say what pushed the paint.

setup.art: A spoon putting a drop of yellow haldi water on a sheet of paper on newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Put a drop of runny paint on the paper.

setup.art: A child blowing through a straw at the drop, which spreads into thin branches like a tree.
setup.caption: 2. Blow through the straw. Watch the paint run.

flow.do: 1. Spread newspaper on the floor. 2. Use the spoon to put a few drops of runny paint near the bottom of the paper.
flow.say: Here are some drops of paint. If you blow at them through this straw, what do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: What will the paint do if you blow on it? Why?

good: It will run away from the straw.

flow.do: Your child blows the drop in different directions. Add more drops and colours if you like.
flow.say: Blow gently, then hard. Which way does the paint go? Can you make it look like a tree, or a firework?
flow.kid: Blow gently. Then blow hard. Which way does the paint go?
flow.parent: The paint runs away from the straw, along the path of the moving air. Hard blows make it go further.

flow.do: Look at the painting together.
flow.say: You never touched the paint. What moved it?
flow.kid: You never touched the paint. What moved it?

activities.title: Bubble Blowing: air inside a bubble
activities.context: In this activity you blow soap bubbles. Each bubble is a thin skin of soapy water with your breath inside. Then you move the air and watch where the bubbles go.

materials.item: a katori of water with 2 spoons of dishwashing liquid stirred in gently

activities.safety: Blow out through the straw. Never suck in. If soap gets in an eye, rinse it with clean water.

schedule.what: Blow bubbles. Fan them with a notebook and watch them float away.

activities.record: Draw a bubble with your breath inside it.

setup.art: A child dipping the end of a straw in a katori of soapy water.
setup.caption: 1. Dip the straw in soapy water.

setup.art: A child gently blowing a big bubble from the straw, while a grown-up fans a floating bubble with a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Blow gently. Then fan the bubbles and watch them go.

flow.do: 1. Dip the end of the straw in the soapy water. 2. Hold it up and blow gently through the other end.
flow.say: Blow very gently. What is inside the bubble?
flow.kid: Blow gently into the straw. What is inside the bubble?
flow.parent: If no bubbles come, add a little more dishwashing liquid and blow more slowly.

flow.do: Your child blows a few bubbles. You fan them gently with the notebook.
flow.say: Watch the bubbles. Which way do they go when I fan them? Can you make them float to the window?
flow.kid: Fan the bubbles. Which way do they go?
flow.parent: The bubbles float along with the moving air, away from the notebook.

flow.do: Ask the last question.
flow.say: We can't see the air inside a bubble. How do we know it is there?
flow.kid: How do we know there is air in a bubble?

ask.q: How do we know there is air inside?
good: The bubble is round and fat.
Something holds it up like a ball.

projects.title: My Air Book: three days
projects.context: In this project you make a small book about air, one page a day. Day 1 is where air is. Day 2 is what moving air pushes. Day 3 is who uses air.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or tied with thread

schedule.what: Make the book. On page 1, draw three places in your home where there is air.
Look out of the window. On page 2, draw three things that moving air pushes.
On page 3, draw three living beings that use air. Show your whole book to someone and tell them about each page.

projects.record: The finished air book, shown to a family member and told page by page.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper folded into a little book, with 'My Air Book' written on the cover in crayon.
setup.caption: 1. Make a little book.

setup.art: An open page with crayon drawings of a cupboard, a bed and a bucket, each with little dots of air inside.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one page each day.

flow.do: 1. Fold and staple the book. 2. Your child writes or copies 'My Air Book' on the cover. 3. On page 1, they draw three places where there is air.
flow.say: Where did we find air? Draw three places on this page. Draw little dots to show the air.
flow.kid: Draw three places where air is. Use dots for the air.

flow.do: Look out of a window together for a few minutes, then draw.
flow.say: Look outside. What is the air pushing? Draw three things on page 2.
flow.kid: Look out of the window. What is the air pushing? Draw three things.
flow.parent: Good things to spot: leaves, clothes on a line, a flag, a kite, smoke, dust, a bird gliding.

flow.do: On page 3, your child draws three living beings that use air. Then they show the book and tell what is on each page.
flow.say: Who uses air? Draw three living beings. Then show your book to a family member and tell them about each page.
flow.kid: Draw three living beings that use air. Show your book to someone.

good: Me, the cat and the tulsi plant.
A crow, because she breathes air.

challenges.title: Sail the Paper Boat Without Touching It
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Fold a paper boat and get it across a tray of water using only moving air.
challenges.problem: Your paper boat is at one end of a tray of water. Get it to the other end without touching the boat or the water.
constraints: Use only air to move the boat.
Don't touch the boat or the water.
materials: a sheet of paper or newspaper, for the boat
a big plate, a tray or a wide basin with a little water
a straw, a notebook, and a plastic bag
general: Blow on the boat from behind.
creative: Add a tall paper sail, so the moving air has more to push.
Blow through a straw at the sail, to aim the air.
Catch air in a bag and squeeze it out behind the boat.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to move the boat with air. Try it. Which way got the boat across in the fewest puffs?

setup.art: A paper boat floating at one end of a steel plate of water.
setup.caption: 1. Put the boat at one end of the tray.

setup.art: A child blowing through a straw at a paper sail on the boat, and the boat moving across.
setup.caption: 2. Move it with air only. No touching!

flow.do: Fold a paper boat together. Put a little water in the tray and float the boat at one end.
flow.say: Can you get the boat to the other end without touching it or the water? How?
flow.kid: Get the boat across. Don't touch it. How will you do it?

flow.do: Let your child try their ideas. Then show the creative ideas one at a time, if they get stuck.
flow.say: Try it. Count your puffs. Now try a sail. Does the boat go faster?
flow.kid: Try it. Count your puffs. Try a sail. Is it faster?
flow.parent: A paper sail on a rolled-paper mast taped to the boat gives the moving air more to push on. A paper boat gets soggy after a while. Make a new one if it does.

flow.do: Ask the last question.
flow.say: Which way got your boat across best? What pushed the boat?
flow.kid: Which way worked best? What pushed the boat?

opts: All around us, indoors and outdoors
quiz.why: Air is everywhere around us, even in a still room and under the bed. Outside, we often feel it more, because it moves.

quiz.p: The clothes on the balcony line are flapping. What is moving them?
quiz.why: Wind is moving air. We cannot see it, but we can see it push the clothes.

quiz.p: You catch air in a bag and twist it shut. Then you press the bag. What happens?
opts: It pushes back on your hands
quiz.why: The air inside takes up room, so the bag pushes back like a soft pillow. A bag with no air goes flat.
A cat breathes in and out all day and all night, like you. A steel plate and a stone don't breathe.

quiz.p: Why do you feel air on your face when you run, but not when you sit still?
opts: Running moves you through the air, so it rushes against your skin
Air only comes out when you run
quiz.why: The air is there all the time. When you run, you move through it, and it presses on your face.

quiz.p: You guess that a closed cupboard has no air. Then you test it, and the bag puffs up. What do you do with your guess?
opts: Say what you really saw, and change your guess
Test again until the bag stays flat
quiz.why: A test shows what is true, even when it is not what we guessed. A wrong guess is how we learn.

quiz.p: A tulsi plant grows on the balcony. How does air get into the plant?
opts: Through tiny holes in their leaves
quiz.why: Leaves have tiny holes, too small to see without a microscope. Air goes in and out through them.

quiz.p: You cannot see the wind. How can you tell which way it is blowing?
opts: Look for blue lines in the air
Watch what it pushes, like leaves, smoke and clothes
quiz.why: Wind pushes things along with it. Leaves, smoke and clothes all lean or move the way the wind is going.

quiz.p: Tall windmills turn and make electricity. What turns them?
quiz.why: Wind is moving air. It pushes the big blades round.

quiz.p: A kite stays up high in the sky. What holds it up?
opts: A hidden string in the sky
Moving air pushing on the kite
quiz.why: Moving air pushes against the kite and holds it up while someone holds the string.

items.p: Is there air here? Put each place in a box.
items.a: All five go in 'Air is here'.
items.why: Every place had air. The bag puffed up even under the bed and inside the bucket. A strong answer puts nothing in 'No air here'.

items.p: Draw the bag twice: when it was squeezed flat and twisted shut, and after you caught air in it.
items.a: A flat, crinkly bag, and a fat, round bag.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference: the bag stayed flat when no air could get in, and puffed up when it scooped air.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'Flat bag' and 'Bag of air'.

items.p: In Blow Painting, you blew at a drop of paint through a straw. What moved the paint?
opts: Your breath, which is moving air
items.why: Your breath is moving air. It pushed the paint along, and you never touched the paint.

items.p: Draw a line from each one to what its moving air does.
pairs: flaps the pages of the calendar
items.why: Each of these moves air. The moving air pushes whatever is in its way.

items.p: We can see the air in a room.
items.why: False. Light goes straight through clean air, so the air is invisible. We feel it when it moves.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: how do you know there is air inside an empty bucket?
items.a: I swept a bag inside the bucket and it puffed up.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the test, the bag puffing up, not just 'because air is everywhere'.

items.p: Here is a balcony on a windy day. Put a W on everything the wind is moving.
items.a: W on the flapping clothes, the swaying plant, the flying kite and the blowing leaves. No W on the flowerpot or the railing.
items.why: Wind pushes light, loose things. A heavy flowerpot and a fixed railing stay still.
items.art: A balcony with clothes flapping on a line, a plant bending, a kite in the sky, leaves blowing, a heavy flowerpot and a steel railing.

items.p: A girl called Kavya sits very still in a room with the fan off. She feels no air on her arm. Why?
opts: There is no air in the room
items.why: The air is there, but it is still. Kavya will feel it when it moves, or when she moves through it.

items.p: Which one is NOT moving air?
items.why: A fan's breeze, your breath and the wind are all moving air. A stone on the floor is not air, and it is not moving.

items.p: Two friends in Madurai look at an empty water bottle with no cap.

views.says: It is empty. There is nothing inside.

items.ask: Who is right? Use what you found in Catch the Air. Then say one thing Divya got right.
items.a: Lakshmi is right: the bottle is full of air, just like the bucket and the space under the bed. Divya is right that there is no water and nothing we can see inside.
items.why: A strong answer uses the bag test: every place that looked empty had air. It is also fair to Divya: 'empty' usually means nothing we can see.

items.p: In Catch the Air, you squeezed the bag flat, twisted it shut and pulled the sides. Why did it stay flat?
opts: Air is too heavy to go in
items.why: With the neck twisted shut, no air could get in, so there was nothing to make the bag fat. This shows that the fat bags really had air in them.

items.p: Put the steps of Catch the Air in the right order.
items: Squeeze it and feel it push back
a: Squeeze it and feel it push back
items.why: You open the bag, scoop the air, close it so the air can't escape, then feel it.

items.p: Draw the air coming out of the bag onto your cheek. Show the moving air with lines.
items.a: A bag near a face, with wavy lines going from the bag's neck to the cheek, and hair lifting.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the air moving from the bag to the cheek. Lines are how we draw air we cannot see.

items.p: Wind is air that is moving.
items.why: True. Wind is moving air. A fan, a waving hand and the weather outside all make wind.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: a paper on the table stays still when the fan is off. When the fan is on, it flies off. Why?
items.a: The fan moves the air, and the moving air pushes the paper.
items.why: A strong answer says it is moving air that pushes the paper. The air was there before, but it was still.

items.p: Fill the gap: We cannot ____ air, but we can feel it when it moves.
items.why: Air is invisible, because light goes straight through it. We feel it when it moves against our skin.

items.p: Here is a child breathing. Draw an arrow for the air going in, and another arrow for the air coming out.
items.a: One arrow going into the nose, and one coming out of the nose or mouth.
items.why: We breathe air in through the nose and mouth, into the chest, and then breathe it out again.
items.art: A child's face and chest drawn from the side, with space around the nose and mouth for arrows.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: the air in your room looks clear, but the sky looks blue. The sky is made of air too. Why might it look blue?
items.a: There is a huge amount of air above us, and so much air sends back some blue light.
items.why: A strong answer says that a little air looks clear, but a very big amount of air looks blue. Any answer that thinks about how much air there is, is a good start.

items.p: Sort these: which does the wind move, and which does it not move on a normal day?
cats: The wind does not move it
items: The wind does not move it
The wind does not move it
items.why: Moving air pushes everything, but it moves light things far more easily than heavy ones. Only a very strong storm moves heavy things.

items.p: In Bubble Blowing, what is inside a bubble you blew?
items.why: A bubble is a thin skin of soapy water with your breath inside. Your breath is air.

applications: Ceiling fans, table fans and palm-leaf hand fans move air onto us to cool us on hot days.
Tall windmills near Kanyakumari and in Gujarat turn in the wind and make electricity.
Kites fly over Ahmedabad at Uttarayan and over many cities at Makar Sankranti, held up by moving air.
Bicycle tyres, footballs and balloons are filled with air, so they are bouncy and firm.
Anna Mani, an Indian scientist, built instruments to measure the air: how fast the wind blows and how much ozone, a gas, is high up in the sky.

open_questions.q: Where does the air end and space begin?
open_questions.why_open: Air gets thinner and thinner the higher you go. There is no sharp edge. Many people use a line 100 kilometres up, but scientists still argue about where the edge should be.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a plant to feel the wind?
open_questions.why_open: Plants feel the wind. A plant that is shaken every day grows shorter and sturdier. Nobody knows yet what feeling the wind is like for the plant.

open_questions.q: Do planets far away have air?
open_questions.why_open: With big telescopes, scientists have found air around some planets that circle other stars. They are still working out what that air is made of, and whether anyone could breathe it.

ask_kids: Where is the air in this room right now?
Can you feel the air at this moment? Why, or why not?
What is the wind pushing outside the window today?
Breathe out on your hand. Is your breath warm or cool?
Who else in our home breathes air?

jokes.j: What is everywhere, but nobody has ever seen it?
Why did the plastic bag go under the bed?
jokes.a: To catch some air down there.

jokes.j: What did the air say to the fan?
What did the bag say when it was full of air?
Why did the kite go to school?
How does a bubble say goodbye?
What did the wind say to the clothes on the line?
What did the empty bucket say?
jokes.a: I'm not empty, I'm full of air!

maths.problem: A girl called Revathi caught air in a bag in 6 places. The bag puffed up in every place. In how many places did she find no air?
maths.answer: 0 places. She found air in all 6 places.
maths.explain: 6 places, and the bag puffed up in 6. 6 take away 6 is 0. So there was no place without air.
maths.context: This is about Catch the Air, where you swept a bag through six places.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the places with air from all the places shows how many had no air, and that number is zero.

maths.problem: In the skin test, a girl called Meena felt 3 out of 3 waves on her cheek, but only 1 out of 3 on the sole of her foot. Where did she feel more? How many more?
maths.answer: On her cheek. She felt 2 more waves there.
maths.explain: 3 is more than 1. 3 take away 1 is 2.
maths.context: This is about the skin test, where a grown-up waved a notebook near different parts of your skin.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows which part of the skin feels moving air better.

maths.problem: In the Cotton Ball Race, a girl called Nisha fanned her ball with a notebook and needed 7 waves. With a bag of air she needed only 4 squeezes. Which way needed fewer? How many fewer?
maths.answer: The bag of air needed fewer. It needed 3 fewer.
maths.explain: 4 is less than 7. 7 take away 4 is 3.
maths.context: This is about the Cotton Ball Race, where you moved a cotton ball with air only.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows which way got the ball to the line with fewer puffs, and by how many.

When it moves against our skin, or when we move through it.

warmup.a: For example, a cat and a tulsi plant. Humans and other animals breathe it, and plants take it in through their leaves.

founder: No by_topic file exists for air. The founder's notebook item phy:63 is 'Atmosphere Basics' (a title only).

ideas/by_topic/gases-evaporation-condensation-solutions.md: 'invisible air', watching smoke swirl in air, breathing practices. Used for the still-and-moving activity, the roots practice and the steam-from-the-cooker spotting card.

Ladder: Level 3 (sci.air.air-around-us.L3) shows that air takes up space and has weight, with the full glass of chana, the syringe, the balloon in a bottle, the straw water thief and Anaxagoras's wine bags. This unit repeats none of those. It leads on to Level 3 by showing that air is everywhere, that the bag fills with something real, and that we feel air only when it moves. Level 3 then asks how much room air takes up and what it weighs.
science: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 101 kilopascals. It acts on the skin from all sides and is constant, so it is not felt.

Skin senses air movement through hair follicle receptors on hairy skin and through touch receptors. The face and lips are very sensitive. The sole of the foot has thick skin and is less sensitive to light touch.

Rayleigh scattering: air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths of sunlight more than long (red) ones. J. Tyndall, 1869, blue light from fine particles in a tube. Lord Rayleigh, 1871 and 1899, showed molecules of air alone could make the sky blue. J. Cabannes, 1915, observed light scattering by dust-free gas in the laboratory. C. V. Raman, voyage on the SS Narkunda, 1921, then work on molecular scattering in Kolkata. The Raman effect, C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan, 1928.
Stomata: pores mostly on the underside of leaves, through which gases enter and leave.
Thigmomorphogenesis: plants shaken or brushed regularly grow shorter and sturdier (M. J. Jaffe, 1973).
Children's ideas about wind: Jean Piaget, The Child's Conception of Physical Causality (1927), recorded young children saying that trees make the wind.
Edge of space: the Kármán line at 100 km is widely used. Some scientists argue for about 80 km.
Exoplanet atmospheres: for example, carbon dioxide detected in the atmosphere of WASP-39b by the James Webb Space Telescope, 2022.

Vaisheshika Sutra 2.1.9 to 2.1.10: touch is the mark of air, and since this touch does not belong to visible things, air is known by an invisible mark. Tao Te Ching 5: the space between heaven and earth is like a bellows.
Anna Mani (1918 to 2001), India Meteorological Department: wind and solar measurement, and an ozonesonde for measuring ozone.
Muppandal wind farm, Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu.

roots.context: We have caught air in a bag in every corner of our home, and felt it on our skin only when it moved. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Sitting still, you felt no air on your skin, yet your bags found air in every corner. When the bag's air rushed out onto your cheek, you felt it at once. Your skin feels air when air moves against it. So air touches you all the time, and you notice it only when it moves.
deep_truth.habit: We think that if something were touching us, we would feel it. But air presses on our skin all day, and we notice only when it moves. Not feeling something does not tell us it is not there.
deep_truth.evidence: In Still Air, Moving Air, a child sitting still with the fan off felt no air at all. In Catch the Air, a bag swept through every place, even under the bed and inside an empty bucket, puffed up. When its air was squeezed out onto the cheek, the child felt it straight away.

three.who_am_i: You are wrapped in air all the time, and some of it is inside you right now, in your chest.
three.what_is_life: Every living being you know uses air: you, the cat, the crow and the tulsi plant.
three.what_is_this_world: A layer of air wraps the whole Earth. There is so much of it that, when we look up, we see it as the blue sky.

roots.thread: One layer of air wraps the whole Earth, with no walls in it. The same air is a sea breeze in Chennai, the breath of a cow in Punjab and the wind over a tea garden in Assam. It goes into you as a breath and comes out again, into the room and the city. Everything is conscious, the moving air too, in its own way. Each breath joins you to all of it.

teachings.teaching: Kanada, a thinker in ancient India, said that touch is the sign of air. The touch we feel in a wind does not belong to anything we can see. So, he said, air is a real thing of its own, known by touch and not by sight.
teachings.link: This is what you found too. Your eyes could not find the air. Your cheek and your hands could.

teachings.teaching: The space between sky and earth is like a bellows. It is empty, yet it never runs out. The more it moves, the more comes out.
teachings.link: A bellows is a bag that pushes out air when you squeeze it, like your bag of caught air. The room looked empty, but each bag you swept through it came back full.

science.text: Air is a mix of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, that wraps the Earth. Its tiny bits fly about and press on everything, from every side, all the time.
The sky is blue because the tiny bits of air send blue sunlight off in all directions more than red sunlight.

other_view.view: Many scientists say air is not aware of anything. Its tiny bits only bump about. They say feeling needs a living body, with nerves or at least living cells.

practice.title: Feel the air you cannot see
practice.say: Sit very still and close your eyes. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Feel the cool air going in. Now breathe out slowly. Feel the warm air coming out. Now hold up one hand and blow on it gently. Feel that? Now be still again. The air is still touching you, all over, even though you can't feel it.
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. Feel the cool air go in. Breathe out. Feel the warm air come out. Blow on your hand. Then be still again.

ask: If you cannot notice something, how could you find out if it is there?
The air you breathed out is in the room now. Is it still a part of you?
What else might be all around us that we cannot see or feel?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed and one palm up, with faint dots of air all around her and one soft curl of breath going in at her nose.

how_we_found_out.context: If air is invisible, why is the sky blue? This card tells the true story of how people found out.
how_we_found_out.story: Clean air is clear, so people long wondered why the sky is blue. Many thought the blue came from dust or tiny drops of water high up. Lord Rayleigh, a scientist in Britain, worked out that very tiny things send blue light off sideways much more than red light. In 1899 he showed that the tiny bits of air themselves are enough to make the sky blue, with no dust at all. In 1921 the Indian scientist C. V. Raman was on a ship to England. He looked at the blue sea and asked if it was blue only because it copied the sky. Back in Kolkata, he and his students shone light through clear water and found that water sends blue light sideways too. So the sea is blue partly by itself. And when you look up at the blue sky, you are seeing air.
how_we_found_out.who: Lord Rayleigh in Britain and C. V. Raman in India
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That clean air has no colour at all, and the sky's blue comes from dust or water drops. Rayleigh showed that the bits of air themselves send blue light our way.
how_we_found_out.art: A man on a ship's deck looking at a deep blue sea under a blue sky.

playtest: Walked the whole unit as a parent and a six-year-old in a Kochi-style flat: both games with 2 and 4 players (all 12 cards and 3 mats listed; game 2 now says what a tied round means and to catch the bag of air first), the bag, skin, paint, bubble and boat activities (minutes add up; the bag test now says 'scoop' in the fair test and the steps, no contradiction), the 3-day air book (the child shows and tells instead of reading), and the quiz (one repeat of the bag test replaced by a new question about guesses). Removed the internal note on the song (the three videos still need checked addresses; the validator requires exactly 3), shortened the Rayleigh and Raman story, and made the mountain climbers' cylinders oxygen.

quiz: A bottle that looks empty is really full of air.
We cannot see air, but it fills every space that looks empty.
Trees make the wind by waving their branches.
Wind is moving air. The branches wave because the wind pushes them.
There is air only outside, where the wind blows.
Air is indoors too. It is just not moving, so we do not feel it.
A fan can make wind in a room that has no trees.
Wind is air that is moving, and a fan makes air move.
We cannot see air because light goes straight through it.
Nothing bounces back to our eyes, so air looks like nothing.
If you cannot feel any air on your skin, there is no air near you.
Still air is not moving against your skin, but it is still there.
Fast moving air pushes harder than slow moving air.
The faster air moves, the harder it pushes whatever is in its way.
Only people need air to live.
All animals breathe air too, and plants take air in as well.
The wind stops being air when it stops blowing.
Wind is just air that is moving. When it stops, the air is still there.
A kite flies high because moving air pushes on it.
Moving air pushes on things, so we can see what the wind does.
odd: We cannot see air, wind or a smell, but we can see a stone.
Wind easily pushes light things, but a big heavy rock is too heavy for wind to move.
A child, a crow and a goat breathe air to stay alive, but a toy car does not.
The first three are full of air. The glass is full of water, so there is no room for air.
Fan breeze, sea breeze and storm wind are moving air we can feel. Still room air is not moving.
